intro: Naples hides three cities stacked on top of one another — Greek, Roman and Baroque — and you'll literally walk over all three along Spaccanapoli, the straight street that has cut the historic centre in half for 2,500 years. You'll hunt for a rose window with no glass, count marble angels above an ancient Greek agora, and decode a facade nobody has ever fully read, while underground Naples keeps beating beneath your feet. It's a little under 2 km, mostly flat.
puntoPartida: Piazza Duomo, in front of the facade of the Cattedrale di San Gennaro (the Duomo di Napoli)

paradas.titulo: The Rose Window With No Glass
paradas.llegada: Standing in Piazza Duomo, facing the facade of the Duomo di Napoli, find the large circular stone rose window set just above the central portal.
paradas.enigma: Most Gothic rose windows are made of coloured glass, to let the light through. This one is a 'rosone cieco' — a blind rose window: sealed and carved from solid stone, with a sculpted figure at its centre instead of glass. Who does that figure represent, its right hand raised in blessing?
pistas: It isn't a local saint — it's the central figure of all Christianity.
Its right hand is raised, in the classic gesture of blessing.
It's Christ (the Cristo Benedicente), blessing from the centre of the rose window.
paradas.historia: The facade in front of you is barely a century old: it's neo-Gothic, designed by Errico Alvino and built between 1877 and 1905, when Naples finally decided to finish a cathedral whose original Gothic facade had stood unfinished for centuries. The three portals are far older — the central one still rests on two 14th-century stone lions by Tino di Camaino, which already held up the original porch.
paradas.fuente: Arcidiocesi di Napoli; Wikipedia — Duomo di Napoli

paradas.titulo: The Saint With the Keys, the Saint With the Sword
paradas.llegada: Go into the Duomo — admission is free — and look along the right-hand nave for the large gilded bronze gate leading into the Cappella del Tesoro di San Gennaro.
paradas.enigma: This gate, the work of sculptor Cosimo Fanzago, took some forty years to complete. On either side of the doorway stand two nearly life-sized white marble statues, carved around 1640 by Giuliano Finelli: they depict two apostles almost always shown together in Christian tradition. One holds a set of keys; the other, a sword. What are these two saints called?
pistas: They're the two apostles the Church celebrates together every 29 June.
The one with the keys founded the Church of Rome; the one with the sword was converted on the road to Damascus.
They are Saint Peter (with the keys) and Saint Paul (with the sword).
paradas.historia: Behind this gate, the altar hides a safe that only opens with two keys at once: one is kept by the Archbishop of Naples, the other by the Deputazione, a lay civic body that has existed since the 16th century and answers to no church authority. Inside are the ampoules holding the blood of San Gennaro, which tradition says liquefies on the Saturday before the first Sunday of May, on 19 September, and on 16 December. Look too at the small bronze columns along the lower part of the gate — Fanzago designed them to ring out like a xylophone when struck, a reminder that this chapel was built for music as well as worship.
paradas.fuente: Museo del Tesoro di San Gennaro; Wikipedia — Cancello di Cosimo Fanzago

paradas.llegada: Leave the Duomo, cross Via Duomo heading west, and enter the long, straight, narrow street that begins right by the junction with Via San Gregorio Armeno.
paradas.enigma: Everyone in Naples calls this street 'Spaccanapoli' — 'the street that splits Naples in two' — because it follows, almost without deviating a single metre, the line of a Greek decumanus laid out 2,500 years ago: look down its length and see just how perfectly straight it runs, far beyond where your eye can follow. But 'Spaccanapoli' is only a popular nickname, not an official name, and it appears on no street sign. Find the plaque with the street's real name on a nearby corner building. What name does it give?
pistas: Don't look for the word 'Spaccanapoli' — it doesn't exist on any sign along the street.
The name combines a saint, Biagio, with the old trade of the booksellers (librai) who once worked here.
The plaque reads Via San Biagio dei Librai.
paradas.historia: Spaccanapoli doesn't carry a single sign with its own name along nearly 2 km of route: its official name changes several times — San Biagio dei Librai, Benedetto Croce, Vicaria Vecchia — without the street bending a single degree. It's the lower decumanus of Greek and then Roman Neapolis, and its straightness is best appreciated from the San Martino viewpoint on the Vomero hill: from up there, this street splits the city clean in two, as if it had been cut with a knife.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Via San Biagio dei Librai; Comune di Napoli

paradas.titulo: The Character Who Wasn't Born in Bethlehem
paradas.llegada: Turn onto Via San Gregorio Armeno, the narrow street running north, its shop windows overflowing with terracotta and wooden figures for the Neapolitan presepe (nativity scene).
paradas.enigma: Among the shepherds, the Three Kings and the Baby Jesus, one character keeps reappearing in almost every window, in dozens of sizes and poses, despite having nothing to do with the Gospel: he wears a loose white jacket and trousers, a black half-mask, and often a pointed cap. What is this mask called — the most famous one in Naples?
pistas: He isn't a shepherd or a king — he's a Commedia dell'Arte mask, born in Naples.
His name may echo 'pulcino' (chick), perhaps for his high-pitched voice and his beak-like curved nose.
He is Pulcinella.
paradas.historia: Pulcinella was born in the 17th century as a Commedia dell'Arte mask and became the comic symbol of the Neapolitan people: lazy, hungry and a bit of a trickster, yet able to survive any disaster with a quick line. This street has kept a craft documented as far back as the 18th century; every year, alongside the classic nativity characters, the workshops add satirical versions of the year's footballers, politicians and celebrities — a tradition of humour with centuries of history behind it in its own right.

paradas.titulo: The Angels Watching Over the Agora
paradas.llegada: Keep climbing Via San Gregorio Armeno until it opens onto Via dei Tribunali, at Piazza San Gaetano: there you'll find a marble column topped by a bronze statue, standing between the basilicas of San Paolo Maggiore and San Lorenzo Maggiore.
paradas.enigma: The column was raised between 1657 and 1664 as a votive offering of thanks after the terrible plague of 1656, which killed a large part of the population of Naples. On the four corners of the marble pedestal are winged figures carved by Andrea Falcone. Count how many marble angels stand at the corners of the pedestal.
pistas: They're on the corners of the marble block, below the bronze statue, not on top of it.
It's the same number as the corners on the pedestal.
There are 4 marble angels, one on each corner.
paradas.historia: The column's original design was by Cosimo Fanzago — the same sculptor behind the gilded gate of the Cappella del Tesoro — though the bronze statue crowning it today is a mid-18th-century replacement. This square is no ordinary square: it occupies the very site of the agora of Greek Neapolis, later the Roman forum. Beneath your feet, in the basement of San Lorenzo Maggiore, the streets and shops of that ancient city are still preserved, and close by is also the entrance to Napoli Sotterranea: the tunnels and cisterns that Greeks and Romans carved into the volcanic tuff starting in the 4th century BC.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Monumento a San Gaetano; Comune di Napoli

paradas.titulo: The Alchemist Prince's Coat of Arms
paradas.llegada: Retrace your steps to Spaccanapoli and continue west to Piazza San Domenico Maggiore. Turn onto Via Francesco De Sanctis, a narrow street on your left, until you reach the sober grey stone facade of the Cappella Sansevero.
paradas.enigma: This chapel holds the Veiled Christ inside, one of the most admired sculptures in Italy — but before you go in, look up above the main portal: there's a carved stone coat of arms of the Di Sangro family, the princes of Sansevero. Count how many diagonal bands cross the shield.
pistas: They're parallel lines, all running diagonally — not vertical, not horizontal.
It's an odd number, greater than one and less than five.
There are 3 diagonal bands.
paradas.historia: The Di Sangro coat of arms is gold with three blue bands. The last and most famous Prince of Sansevero, Raimondo di Sangro (1710–1771), turned this family chapel into a labyrinth of Masonic and alchemical symbols: he was credited with inventions as varied as a waterproof fabric and an ink that never fades, and the Church went as far as placing his writings on Freemasonry on the Index of banned books. It was he who commissioned the Veiled Christ, which today draws a queue of visitors every morning before opening.
paradas.fuente: Museo Cappella Sansevero; Wikipedia — Raimondo di Sangro

paradas.titulo: The Facade Nobody Has Ever Read
paradas.llegada: Continue along Via Benedetto Croce to Piazza del Gesù Nuovo. There you'll find a facade like no other in Naples: an entire wall covered in grey stones carved to a point, as if bristling with spikes.
paradas.enigma: This technique is called 'bugnato a punta di diamante' — diamond-point rustication: each block of piperno stone isn't simply pointed, it's carved into the shape of a small square-based pyramid. Get close to just one stone, at hand height, and look carefully at its shape. How many triangular faces does each diamond-point stone have?
pistas: Don't count the base, flush against the wall — count only the faces that project outward.
It's the same number as the sides of the square base the pyramid rises from.
Each stone has 4 triangular faces.
paradas.historia: On some of these same stones are carved marks — letters, symbols, strokes — that nobody has ever fully explained. One theory, published after years of study, suggests a group of them reproduces seven signs from an Aramaic alphabet once used to notate music, as if the facade were hiding a musical score; other historians believe they're stonemasons' tally marks, used to count finished stones and calculate pay. This building was once a Renaissance palace, the Palazzo Sanseverino, until the Jesuits acquired it in the late 16th century and built the church behind the facade, keeping it almost untouched: only three other diamond-point facades like this one are known in the world, two in Italy and one in Barcelona.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Chiesa del Gesù Nuovo; Vanilla Magazine — La partitura enigma del Gesù Nuovo

paradas.titulo: The Flowers That Arrive by Ladder
paradas.llegada: In the same square, turn towards the white marble spire rising in front of the church: the Guglia dell'Immacolata, completed in 1750.
paradas.enigma: This spire was funded by alms collected by a Neapolitan Jesuit and built in under three years. At the top, almost 30 metres above the square, stands a gilded bronze statue. Who does the figure crowning the entire spire represent?
pistas: It's the same figure the whole square and the church next to it are dedicated to.
'Immaculate' means that, by Catholic dogma, she was born without original sin.
It's the Immaculate Conception (the Virgin Mary).
paradas.historia: Every 8 December, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, Naples firefighters climb a fire-truck's telescopic ladder all the way to the top and place a bunch of roses in the hands of this bronze Virgin, the work of Francesco Pagano, in front of thousands of onlookers — a tradition still kept alive well into the 21st century. Lower down, on the first-level balustrade, four statues of Jesuit saints by Matteo Bottiglieri keep watch over the square, one last reminder that in Naples, devotion and street spectacle have been the same thing for centuries.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Napoli; Wikipedia — Guglia dell'Immacolata

final.titulo: You Have Split Naples in Two
final.texto: From a rose window with no glass to a spire firefighters still decorate by hand every December, you've walked a little under 2 km over a Greek decumanus, a chapel with two keys that neither opens alone, and a facade nobody has ever fully decoded. Spaccanapoli still splits the city in two, just as it did 2,500 years ago — and now you also know why the name everyone uses appears on no sign at all.
